subskill: boundaries: comma splice disguised by a having-phrase opening the second clause
passage: For months before the eruption, seismometers on the volcano's southern slope recorded the lava dome swelling by nearly a meter each ______ dome collapsed without warning in late March, releasing a lateral blast that flattened mature forest more than ten kilometers from the vent and buried the valley below in ash.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: week; having finally outgrown its crater, the
week, having finally outgrown its crater, the
week, having finally outgrown its crater. The
week having finally outgrown its crater, the
correct_answer: week; having finally outgrown its crater, the
explanation: The text contains two independent clauses: "seismometers ... recorded the lava dome swelling by nearly a meter each week" and "the dome collapsed without warning." The participial phrase "having finally outgrown its crater" belongs to the second clause and describes the dome. "week; having finally outgrown its crater, the" places a semicolon between the clauses and leaves the phrase introducing "the dome," which it modifies. "week, having finally outgrown its crater, the" joins the two independent clauses with only a comma, a comma splice. "week having finally outgrown its crater, the" runs the clauses together with no mark at all. "week, having finally outgrown its crater. The" puts the period after the phrase, attaching it to the first sentence, where it can only modify that sentence's subject, "seismometers"; the seismometers did not outgrow a crater (and the singular "its" cannot refer back to them), so the modifier dangles.

subskill: boundaries: closing a long dash-set modifier between subject and main verb
passage: The navigational compass of the migrating monarch butterfly—a time-compensated mechanism that integrates the sun's position in the sky with signals from a circadian clock located partly in each ______ remains accurate enough over a journey of nearly two months to guide insects that have never made the trip to a few small groves of fir trees thousands of kilometers to the south.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the sentence is "The navigational compass of the migrating monarch butterfly," and its verb is "remains." Between them sits a long nonrestrictive modifier, "a time-compensated mechanism ... located partly in each antenna," which opens with a dash. A modifier opened with a dash must close with a dash, so "antenna—" is correct and returns the reader to the main clause. "antenna," closes the modifier with a comma, mismatching the pair. "antenna;" separates the subject from its verb, leaving "The navigational compass ... antenna" as a fragment with no verb and "remains accurate ..." as a clause with no subject. "antenna" leaves the dash pair unclosed and makes the main verb "remains" appear to belong to "each antenna" inside the modifier, so the subject "compass" never gets a verb.

subskill: boundaries: closing a comma-set relative clause that contains a nested dash pair
passage: The psalter's principal scribe, who—unusually for a monastic copyist of that era—signed and dated each finished ______ illustrated the margins himself, filling them with grotesques and hybrid beasts that later cataloguers mistook for the work of a second, more accomplished hand. Only in 2009 did ink analysis show that a single batch of iron-gall ink had been used for both the text and the drawings.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject "The psalter's principal scribe" is followed by a nonrestrictive relative clause, "who ... signed and dated each finished quire," which opens with a comma and contains its own dash pair ("—unusually for a monastic copyist of that era—"). The dash pair is already closed, so the relative clause must now close with a comma, matching the comma that opened it; the main verb "also illustrated" then follows. "quire, also" does this. "quire—also" closes a comma-opened element with a dash, mismatching the pair. "quire; also" places a semicolon between the subject and its verb, leaving "The psalter's principal scribe, who ... quire" as a fragment. "quire, and also" makes "illustrated" a second verb inside the relative clause or a verb joined by "and" to nothing, so the subject "scribe" never receives a main verb.

subskill: boundaries: colon before a long, internally punctuated noun-phrase series
passage: Because snow falling on the ice sheet traps air and dust as it compacts, a single core drilled through the ice preserves several independent records of past climate, all aligned in one ______ bubbles of ancient air, whose carbon dioxide can be measured directly; layers of volcanic ash, which can be dated against known eruptions; and ratios of oxygen isotopes, which track the temperature at which each year's snow formed.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The text before the blank is an independent clause that mentions "several independent records of past climate." What follows is not a clause but a long series of noun phrases ("bubbles of ancient air ...; layers of volcanic ash ...; and ratios of oxygen isotopes ...") that specifies those records, with semicolons separating its internally punctuated items. A colon is the mark that introduces such a list after a complete clause, so "column: bubbles" is correct. "column. Bubbles" leaves the series standing alone as a sentence with no main verb, a fragment. "column; bubbles" also fails, because a semicolon must be followed by an independent clause or by another item in a semicolon series, and the series has not begun. "column, bubbles" makes the list read as an appositive renaming "one column," which it cannot do (a column is not bubbles, ash, and isotope ratios), and a comma cannot introduce a series whose items are separated by semicolons.

subskill: boundaries: however as an interrupter after a long verbless introductory phrase
passage: Designers of the first biplanes assumed that stacking two identical wings would roughly double an aircraft's lift. In the wind-tunnel trials that a pair of engineers ran on scale models of such machines during ______ the lower wing of a typical model generated barely half the lift of the upper wing, because it sat in the disturbed air flowing off the wing above it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The second sentence is a single independent clause, "the lower wing of a typical model generated barely half the lift," preceded by a long introductory prepositional phrase, "In the wind-tunnel trials that a pair of engineers ran ... during 1910." Although that phrase contains the verb "ran," it sits inside a relative clause, so the phrase itself is not a clause. "However" interrupts the sentence to signal contrast with the designers' assumption, and an interrupter is set off by a pair of commas: "1910, however," is correct. "1910; however," treats the introductory phrase as an independent clause, but "In the wind-tunnel trials ... during 1910" has no subject and main verb of its own, so it is a fragment. "1910 however," omits the comma that should open the interrupter. "1910, however" omits the comma that should close it, so "however" runs into "the lower wing" and reads as "in whatever way."

subskill: boundaries: semicolon before a whether-clause subject opening the second clause
passage: Potters have known for centuries that a copper glaze fired in a kiln starved of oxygen emerges a deep blood red instead of the usual ______ the red comes from tiny particles of metallic copper or from a reduced oxide of the metal remained disputed until the 1980s, when electron microscopes finally resolved the particles directly.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The text contains two independent clauses. The first ends with "instead of the usual green." The second has a whole clause as its subject, "whether the red comes from tiny particles of metallic copper or from a reduced oxide of the metal," and "remained disputed" as its verb. A semicolon properly joins two independent clauses, so "green; whether" is correct. "green, whether" joins the two clauses with only a comma, a comma splice; read instead as an adverbial "whether ... or ..." clause attached to the first sentence, it leaves "remained disputed" with no subject. "green whether" runs the clauses together with no punctuation. "green, as to whether" turns the whether-clause into the object of the prepositional phrase "as to," so it can no longer serve as a subject, and "remained disputed" again has nothing to agree with.

subskill: boundaries: preposition needed to attach a verbless noun phrase to the clause
passage: Because the speed of sound in seawater reaches a minimum about a kilometer below the surface, sound waves near that depth are bent back toward it whenever they stray upward or downward. A low-frequency call trapped in this channel can therefore cross an entire ocean ______ little loss of strength over thousands of kilometers, since seawater absorbs sound at such frequencies only weakly.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: After the independent clause "A low-frequency call ... can therefore cross an entire ocean basin," the rest of the sentence is a noun phrase, "remarkably little loss of strength over thousands of kilometers," followed by a subordinate "since" clause; it contains no main verb of its own. The preposition "with" attaches that noun phrase to the clause as a description of how the call crosses the basin, so "basin with remarkably" is correct. "basin. Remarkably" and "basin; remarkably" both cut the noun phrase off from the clause; "Remarkably little loss of strength ..., since seawater absorbs sound ..." has no subject-verb pair outside its "since" clause, so each option leaves a fragment. "basin, remarkably" leaves the noun phrase dangling after a comma with nothing to connect it: it cannot be an appositive, because "little loss of strength" does not rename "an entire ocean basin," and it has no participle that would make it an absolute phrase.

subskill: boundaries: no mark between verb + object complement and its delayed object
passage: For decades, the fungi that partner with plant roots could be studied only indirectly, through chemical traces they left in soil samples. A staining technique developed in a university soil laboratory changed that. Applied to a thin slice of undisturbed earth, the new dye makes visible to anyone with an ordinary light ______ thread-like fungal filaments that link the root tips of neighboring plants into a single underground network.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The verb phrase "makes visible" needs an object, and here that object ("the thread-like fungal filaments that link ...") has been moved after the long phrase "to anyone with an ordinary light microscope." Nothing may separate a verb from its object, so "microscope the" is correct. "microscope, the" inserts a comma between the verb and its object. "microscope. The" leaves "the new dye makes visible to anyone with an ordinary light microscope" without an object and turns the rest into a fragment, since "The thread-like fungal filaments that link ..." has no main verb ("link" belongs to the relative clause). "microscope and the" folds the filaments into the phrase "anyone with an ordinary light microscope and the ... filaments," so "makes visible" again has no object.

subskill: boundaries: comma + coordinating conjunction before a clause that opens with a subordinate clause
passage: Printed partbooks, which gave each singer a separate volume containing a single voice, let a motet travel far beyond the chapel where it was first performed. These editions preserved the composer's pitches and rhythms ______ printers seldom showed exactly which syllable of the Latin text belonged beneath which note, singers in different cities had to settle that alignment for themselves.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The sentence contains two independent clauses: "These editions preserved the composer's pitches and rhythms faithfully" and "singers in different cities had to settle that alignment for themselves." The second is preceded by the introductory clause "because printers seldom showed ... note." Two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction take a comma before the conjunction, so "faithfully, but because" is correct. "faithfully, because" makes the "because" clause modify the first clause and then joins "singers ... had to settle" with only a comma, a comma splice. "faithfully but because" and "faithfully but, because" both omit the required comma before "but" between the two independent clauses; the comma after "but" in the latter does not replace it.

subskill: boundaries: colon introducing an independent clause the first clause announces
passage: Historians had long treated a 1570s chart of the Breton coast as a straightforward copy of an earlier map. But when conservators examined the sheet under raking light, the faint guidelines beneath its ink revealed something no scholar had ______ the mapmaker had first sketched the shoreline as seen from a ship offshore and only later corrected it against surveys made on land.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "The faint guidelines ... revealed something no scholar had anticipated" is a complete clause that announces a discovery, and "the mapmaker had first sketched the shoreline ..." is an independent clause stating what that discovery was. A colon correctly introduces such an explanation, so "anticipated: the" is correct. "anticipated, the" joins the two independent clauses with only a comma, a comma splice. "anticipated the" runs them together with no punctuation; "the mapmaker" cannot serve as the object of "anticipated" because "had first sketched the shoreline" follows it as a second verb with its own object. "anticipated, which the" opens a relative clause, but "which the mapmaker had first sketched the shoreline" has no gap for "which" to fill, since "sketched" already has its object, "the shoreline."

subskill: boundaries: dash before a long sentence-final summarizing appositive
passage: Over six years of monitoring, researchers found that reef patches shaded by overhanging mangroves bleached less often during marine heat waves and, when they did bleach, regained their symbiotic algae within weeks rather than ______ a pattern that suggests coastal forests, which have been widely cleared for shrimp farming, may serve as refuges for corals in a warming ocean.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "A pattern that suggests coastal forests ... may serve as refuges" is not a clause: it is the noun "pattern" followed by a relative clause, and the verb "may serve" belongs to "coastal forests" inside that relative clause. The phrase is an appositive summarizing the finding described before it, and a dash correctly sets off such an appositive at the end of a sentence, so "months—a pattern" is correct. "months. A pattern" and "months; a pattern" each require a complete sentence or independent clause after the mark, leaving "A pattern that suggests ... ocean" as a fragment. "months a pattern" runs the appositive into the clause with no punctuation, so "rather than months a pattern" cannot be parsed.

subskill: boundaries: semicolon + conjunctive adverb between independent clauses
passage: Engineers who built the valley's first railway in the 1830s butted each iron rail tightly against the next, and in summer heat that line buckled so often that trains were regularly ______ the extension laid eleven years later along the same river, whose rails were set with a narrow gap at every joint, ran through even the hottest seasons without a single reported failure.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "In summer heat that line buckled so often that trains were regularly halted" and "the extension laid eleven years later ... ran through even the hottest seasons" are independent clauses. "However" is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot join them by itself; a semicolon before it is required, and a comma follows it. "halted; however," is therefore correct. "halted, however," joins the two clauses with only commas, a comma splice. "halted however," and "halted however" provide no punctuation between the clauses at all, producing run-on sentences (in the former, "however" can attach only to the first clause, leaving the second joined by a comma).

subskill: boundaries: closing comma of a long nonrestrictive clause with internal commas, between subject and verb
passage: Primatologists long assumed that great apes share food chiefly with close relatives. Yet the bonobo community at one long-term field station, which observers have followed almost daily since the late 1970s and which, unlike most wild groups studied so far, has never been given supplementary food by ______ shares meat with unrelated females at least as often as with kin.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject "the bonobo community at one long-term field station" is followed by a nonrestrictive relative clause that opens with a comma ("which observers have followed ... and which ... has never been given supplementary food by humans"); the commas around "unlike most wild groups studied so far" are a separate pair nested inside it. The main verb is "shares," and the relative clause must be closed with a second comma before it, so "humans, shares" is correct. "humans—shares" closes a comma-opened element with a dash, a mismatched pair. "humans; shares" separates the subject from its verb with a semicolon, leaving neither side an independent clause. "humans shares" leaves the relative clause unclosed.

subskill: boundaries: period before a clause opening with an "only after" inversion
passage: Workshops in the eastern Mediterranean produced a brilliant, colorfast red on cotton through a sequence of more than a dozen baths in oil, alkali, and dye, the exact order of which was closely guarded by the dyers' ______ several of these artisans were recruited by French manufacturers in the 1740s did western European mills begin producing the color themselves.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The inverted verb "did western European mills begin" shows that "only after several of these artisans were recruited ..." is fronted to open a new independent clause ("Only after X did mills begin"). That clause must be separated from the first independent clause, which ends with "the dyers' guilds," and a period does so, so "guilds. Only after" is correct. "guilds, only after" joins the two independent clauses with only a comma, a comma splice. "guilds only after" runs them together; "guarded ... only after" cannot absorb the phrase, because "did western European mills begin" is left with no clause to belong to. "guilds, although only after" makes the second clause subordinate, but the subject-auxiliary inversion "did ... mills begin" is not possible in an "although" clause.
